en: Am I awake, or is this a dream?
Has God truly granted it?
My Kulchoro, small as a knucklebone,
From Toltoy, huge as a mountain,
Have you truly escaped and returned?
Have my eyes truly seen you?
My figure standing before me,
My support left to me
By the lions who ruled as kings!”
The prince went to him sobbing;
They met safe and sound,
And he welcomed the boy.
“Ah, Almighty, Babedin!
For a boy such as you,
I would sacrifice my dark life!”
When the prince said this,
The boy said:
“My dear elder,
For a heroic elder like you,
I would sacrifice my dark life!
On hard ground there is no cradle;
I let the fleeing enemy escape—
For wretched me there is no blessed portion.
In a level place there is no cradle;
I let the departing enemy escape—
For wretched me there is no blessed portion.
Blue-maned elder, do not grieve.
May I sink away unborn;
Rather than live powerless,
May I die and live no more!
My dear elder,
Had you not thrust your spear without measure,
Had he not made his spear lunge,
Would I not have undone
Swaggering Toltoy's stratagem?
A blue haze gathered in the sky;
Your Toltoy who came to the frontier
Fled openly and escaped.
A black cloud gathered;
Your Toltoy who came to take a wife—
May this wretched world come to ruin—
Fled plainly and escaped.
At swaggering Toltoy
I thrust twelve spears at once.
The bronze lance in my hand
I spared through my inexperience;
Father, alas, what shall I do?
I spared it through childishness.
Toltoy fled; I thrust at him,
And I was left helpless and empty-handed.
When He makes a mortal, He makes a giant;
Rather than make a person powerless,
Why does Almighty God
Not leave him uncreated?
I reached him and thrust my stout spear;
This poor head, born for hardship,
Let the fleeing enemy get away.
Here is sovereign Afghan land;
Who let the fleeing enemy escape!
Here am I, poor Choro!
Here is the Argyn people with cities;
Elder, here I am if you would spill my blood!”
When his companion said this,
His prince stood and said:
“For a boy like you, small as a crow,
My dear loyal companion,
I would sacrifice my dark life!
His deeds have much left unfinished;
At twelve, a boy is still a child.
He has not yet turned a thoroughbred's head
Or shouted and leveled a spear.
Your words sweeter than sugar—
Almighty God will show them
To your own eyes for certain!
He ordained that I would not be diminished;
The Almighty Himself made me.
I was God's beloved servant;
I was poor Manas's son.
Among horses fit to catch and ride,
There is no mighty mount but Buurul;
Before God, there is no kinsman
For whom I would bow but you!
My bright star in the sky,
My dear Kulchoro,
The precious sable at my collar.
When laid before me, my white road;
My cherished shade,
When following behind me, my countless host.
Seeing you today, my heart is full.
My gift left to me
By my blue-maned foster father—
I have no kinsman but you!
To cast shade as we travel,
My mighty, leafy poplar,
My great support, vast as a mountain,
My great hammer made of gold!
My irrigation channel bearing a river,
The one beneath whose protection I sit,
Kulchoro, my light.
Foot-mist rising from a hollow—
Toltoy, who took the spear wound,
My dear Kulchoro,
Will not escape you tomorrow!
If you did not spear him today,
You will spear him tomorrow.
If you did not bring him hell today,
You will bring him hell tomorrow!”
Comforting Choro with these words,
To the treasured camp,
To the delight of the people,
He led the boy inside,
Into Aychürök's palace.
Aychürök's white palace—
When they reached the white palace,
For a boy such as he,
They had nine black calves
Cut down,
And offered them in sacrifice.
Saying Kulchoro had returned,
With a celebration no one could devise,
All Khan Akun's people—
Those who slaughtered mares slaughtered mares;
Those who slaughtered camels slaughtered camels.
They held a great public feast.
For Khan Akun's daughter,
They had the treasury opened,
And countless red-gold coins
Scattered in largesse.
Every widow who reached them received some;
Every orphan and young child
Received red-gold treasure.
They sold it to shopkeepers,
And the walnuts they bought,
The orphan children then
Threw about the street.
They pledged a sheep to Koroson;
All the people gathered,
The khan's people held a feast
And stayed there rejoicing.
Your guest, brave Semetey—
Now let me tell
The tale of brave Toltoy.
Chynkozho, son of Shygay,
Was like tempered iron;
Brave Toltoy was the courageous one,
His strength equal to half a mountain.
Would Kalcha and Kadyrbay
Stand merely watching,
Without making arrows rain again?
Tölök and Tölöbay
Were the finest of the lower army,
The most skillful at thrusting spears.
Wounded Toltoy's
Pain subsided;
His eyes, huge as felt sacks, opened.
After putting on his bulletproof coat,
The swaggering leopard—
After Toltoy mounted his horse,
The great host of black Jediger
Divided into troop after troop;
Their wrestlers appeared,
Holding clubs as large as houses.
They put bulletproof coats on them
And mounted their heroes on horses.
They set apart those riding gray horses,
The fattest, swaying ponderously;
They set apart those riding duns,
Long-maned and mare-bellied;
They set apart those riding bays,
All thoroughbreds, the very fattest;
They set apart those riding chestnuts,
Which looked as small as falcon hoods;
They set apart those riding kula horses,
Who would enter together and encircle;
They set apart those riding piebalds,
Yellow-mottled like starlings;
They set apart those riding black piebalds,
With smooth, full tails.
Their numbers filled every count;
The time had come
To engulf Afghanistan and fight.
Dust whirled into the sky;
At the call to battle, their heroes
Spurred forward and poured out.
They set apart the heroes
Riding red bay horses,
Their horsehair tails tied tight.
They set apart their finest men,
Who would not stir when a gun struck.
They set apart the capable ones,
Who would not bend when a club struck.
They set apart the hardy ones,
Who would not sway when a whip struck.
They set apart the courageous ones,
Who would steep themselves in black blood
And fight without fleeing.
They set apart the peerless,
The finest among spearmen.
They set apart their best men,
Who knew the enemy's stratagems well.
They set apart those who would not flee
When the black gun cracked.
They set apart those who would not start
When the fierce gun snapped.
They set apart the peerless men ready with spears,
Those who said,
“Our venture rests with Almighty God.”
Their marksmen were at the front;
Their heroes were at the flanks.
Their hardy men were at the front;
Their tigers were at the flanks.
Their spearmen were at the front;
Their lions were at the flanks.
Without twitching the horses' mouths,
Many here wheeled their mounts.
Holding spears and fitting banner tips,
Many here stood ready.
Steeping themselves in bloody blood,
Fighting without fleeing,
Many here were warriors.
Streaming along the riverbank,
Surging across the ground,
They were told, “All advance abreast;
Ride with room and do not collide.”
Spearheads clashed;
Men's heads knocked together.
Commanders of ten swept forward;
Commanders of a hundred towered.
Their ancient fury stirred;
They became an army of many thousands.
They had horns and trumpets sounded,
Loaded troops upon rhinoceroses,
Loaded ammunition on elephants,
And gathered all the Jediger people
To carry out merciless slaughter
And seize Aychürök.
They went to exact, bit by bit,
The vengeance of wounded Toltoy.
The drum's voice thundered;
The brass horn's voice rang.
The gray-mottled pennant became their banner;
A wailing clamor arose.
The white-mottled pennant became their banner;
The air filled with battle cries and clamor.
Toltoy of the Jediger,
His countless army bending the earth—
His spearmen were at the front;
The lion Toltoy was at the flank.
He was driving them forth;
Swarming like ants,
They came seething out.
It was impossible to tell if they were worms,
Impossible to tell if they were people;
They came seething out.
Their heroes were at the front;
Renowned Kozho was at the flank.
